contentBlocks.text: This week you've studied comparative religion's approach. Today: apply that same respectful lens to your own tradition!

A comparative-religion mindset isn't only useful for understanding other traditions, it can also help someone understand their own tradition more clearly, by asking the same kinds of questions: which universal human questions does it address, and how? Using this week's three universal questions (the divine, ethical living, and what happens after death) and last week's Sikh philosophy content (Ik Onkar, Naam Simran, Maya, Hukam), write a short paragraph explaining how Sikhi addresses at least two of these three universal questions.
You just applied comparative-religion thinking to your own tradition! Tomorrow we'll review everything from this week.

objectives: Apply the comparative-religion framework of universal questions to Sikhi specifically
Write a paragraph connecting at least two universal questions to specific Sikh philosophical concepts
materialsNeeded: This week's earlier worksheets, last week's Sikh-philosophy worksheets
teacherGuide.facilitationScript:
1. Review this week's universal-questions and civic-life work.
2. Review last week's four Sikh philosophy concepts briefly.
3. Have the child write their connecting paragraph.
4. Complete the worksheet.
5. Preview tomorrow's cumulative review.
differentiationTips: Struggling: pair one concept with one question first (Ik Onkar with the divine question) as a model before asking for a second independent pairing
Ready for more: ask the child whether Hukam connects more to the ethical-living question or a different one, and why
This is the week's synthesis moment — using an academic framework to understand one's own tradition more clearly is a genuinely valuable skill
teacherGuide.answerKey: This is an open-ended synthesis activity — check that the paragraph genuinely connects at least two universal questions to specific Sikh concepts, for example: Ik Onkar addresses the nature of the divine (oneness), and Hukam addresses ethical living (accepting divine order while still acting responsibly).
teacherGuide.standardsRationale: Directly addresses this course's comparative-religion and Sikh-philosophy threads together, synthesizing both weeks' content before tomorrow's review.
